Ethereum is taking the first step toward protecting staking from quantum attacks.

Here's how it would work:

1. Right now, ETH validators use BLS keys to sign blocks and help secure the network. Those are the keys quantum computers could one day threaten.

2. The proposal would update Ethereum’s validator deposit contract so new staking deposits can support different, quantum-resistant key types in the future.

3. At first, nothing changes for existing validators. BLS deposits would still be accepted while the new systems are tested and rolled out.

4. After a future upgrade, validators could begin depositing with the new signature schemes alongside the old BLS format.

5. Eventually, Ethereum could flip a permanent switch to stop accepting new BLS-based validator deposits entirely, which is the final stage shown in the image.

I think this is a good step in being proactive for @ethereum.

There’s a lot of doomposting about it on my timeline, but quantum computing isn’t inherently bad. Like AI, it can be used for both good and bad.

And while the security risks are real, there will also be a lot of positives that come from it. I’ll probably make my next post about some of those.

this is misleading in 3 major ways. Ronan completely misrepresents how data centers are taxed. 

1. it's uncommon to impose sales taxes on datacenters, for a very ordinary tax policy reason
2. data centers pay far more in taxes than just sales taxes - property taxes, corporate income taxes, tangible personal property, corporate income tax, gross receipts tax. 
3. Georgia is not unusually lenient tax wise 

1. DCs are often rightfully exempt from sales taxes 

so data centers actually seldom pay sales taxes. this makes sense. sales tax is meant to fall on the final consumer, not an intermediate process. (that's not my opinion, that's just the tax policy consideration). a data center buying GPUs is not the final sale. the final sale is the consumer buying a subscription from OpenAI. 

there's a reason we don't impose sales taxes on intermediate goods. you don't tax the wheat / the flour / the oven / the trucks. you just impose a sales tax on the final loaf of bread. otherwise you end up with multiple taxes embedded in the price of the loaf and a massively extractive tax system. 

the same with GPUs. they are an intermediate input into a finished product which is a token delivered to a consumer. our tax system only approximates this and sometimes businesses and states have to negotiate. generally the answer is to waive sales taxes. in a study by the tax foundation only 1 of 12 states contemplated (CA) charged sales taxes to a datacenter [1]. 

the sales tax is not foregone entirely, it is just charged to the person or business consuming the final product. 

also consider that if Georgia were to try and charge this tax, the DCs would just site themselves somewhere else, because most other states also don't impose this specific tax. 

not to mention, even if the sales taxes were imposed, Georgia already has ANOTHER tax break [2] which contemplated this same principle (of not taxing intermediate computer goods). this is the older "High-Technology Computer Equipment exemption" which would give a tech company an exemption from most of the sales taxes on computer equipment purchased. a jan 2026 analysis [3] from the same group Ronan cites concludes that eliminating sales tax would not produce the "$474m in sales taxes" Ronan cites because 82.4% of equipment purchases would be excludable based on the prior exemption. so even if sales taxes were reimposed, it's not like datacenters would magically start paying all those taxes. so the $474m he's complaining about is largely fictitious. 

2. sales taxes are just one piece of the puzzle 

data centers pay wayyyy more in taxes than just sales taxes (which they often don't pay, by design). 

an analysis from the tax foundation [1] looking at 12 common jurisdictions found that the main tax burdens for DCs were property taxes, corporate income tax, and tangible personal property. of those 12 jurisdictions, sales taxes only amounted to 13.7% of a datacenter's tax burden on average (since they are so frequently waived). so Ronan is complaining about the waiver of an infrequently imposed tax while ignoring the very significant taxes paid by datacenters. a billion-dollar datacenter in Atlanta GA, for instance, will pay roughly $108m in taxes over a decade to state and local governments, according to that analysis (excluding federal taxes!). and assuming NO sales tax. of that $108m paid to local and state, it's 58m in property tax, $34m in tangible personal property tax, $16m in electricity sales tax. the city county and state authorities are still very much benefiting fiscally from these datacenters. 

so Ronan's analysis of $474m in foregone sales taxes vs only $41m back from the industry is wrong on both counts. Georgia would have never collected that $474m; DCs were mostly shielded from it anyway even if the special data center exemption was repealed. the audit Ronan cites does not consider the whole tax picture of local/municipal/city/state - it ignores property taxes, which is a majority a GA-based datacenter's tax bill!  

as Ronan notes, at least 38 states waive sales taxes for DCs, which should tip you off that what's going on is not some super unusual bespoke tax break but in fact a very ordinary, widespread tax policy: not taxing intermediate computer equipment. sales taxes are a consumption tax. a datacenter buying servers or GPUs is not consuming. those are business inputs to a subsequent product. these are exempt for the broader tax policy reason of avoiding tax pyramiding. 

3. Georgia isn't particularly lenient 

so is Georgia super lenient in its tax treatment of datacenters? not really! 

looking again at the tax foundation's analysis (last picture), a datacenter in Atlanta GA has a totally middle of the pack state+local tax burden. Georgia isn't some kind of bizarre tax haven for datacenters.

thread_tweets.text:
this stuff is super complicated and most people are new to the state/local/federal tax analysis so of course headlines like "datacenters get massive tax waivers" are compelling. ordinary people _feel_ that they're being cheated by big tech. they read about massive waivers (always these kind of vague, counterfactual estimates that require a ton of contextualization) and assume that DCs are paying no tax. reality couldn't be further from the truth. DCs pay a whole cluster of taxes, and the state/local/city authorities are _always_, unless something has gone horrifyingly wrong, coming out ahead fiscally speaking. 

think about it like this. if you got a personal sales tax waiver, and you didn't have to pay any sales taxes for a year, would you be paying 0 tax? 

of course not. you'd still have to pay property tax, income tax, motor fuel excise tax, utility tax, etc etc etc. datacenters are no different. and Georgia isn't even particularly lenient tax wise.

In the next two or three years, every human could have a hundred... maybe a thousand agents working for them onchain.

Arpan Nanavati breaks it down perfectly in this clip... the whole thing is a cost  curve.

Right now, it costs about $10 a day in inference to run an agent... hedge fund territory. But inference costs have already dropped 100x in three years, and every step down changes who can afford to play:

At $1 a day, every protocol is running agents

At cents a day, your wallet has agents built in, managing your idle capital

At microcents, you get agent swarms

Jevons paradox... every time the cost of something collapses, usage explodes. 

Intelligence is scaling, and theres no reason the number of agents executing onchain cant scale near infinitely.

Madness.

They don’t know how to do it.  They don’t do it in the way I described in the Work Principles part of my book, “Principles: Life and Work”. 

In an idea meritocracy, the boss’s authority is not the absolute and not-to-be-questioned source of believability; track records and logical reasoning are. When people respond to people’s titles and authorities without understanding and thinking about whether the directions being set are logical ones, they have slipped into a ‘not thinking and just following’ mode, which is bad for everyone, and when they think the boss is following a bad path and choose not to explore that with the leader, they have slipped into a submissive follower role, which doesn’t help anyone. Both are bad. 

The fix is to have an open, idea-meritocratic, believability-weighted culture in which to make believability criteria objective, taking into consideration past track records, clear cause‑effect explanations, and transparent data.  Then use agreed‑upon protocols that support this approach (e.g., weighted voting, believability scores) to resolve disagreements. If those rules are followed consistently, the system stays meritocratic; if they’re ignored, it reverts to power rules, and people mindlessly follow.
